solutionMd:
## The idea

Ask each subtree: "do you contain p or q?" A subtree returns p, q, their LCA, or null. If the **left and right** both return something, p and q are on different sides — this node is the LCA. Otherwise pass up whichever side found something.

## Step by step

1. If the node is null, p or q → return it.
2. left = Find(left subtree), right = Find(right subtree).
3. Both non-null → return this node.
4. Else return the non-null one (or null).

## Worked example

**Input:** tree [3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4], p = 5, q = 1

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| at 5 | is p → return 5 |
| at 1 | is q → return 1 |
| at 3 | left gave 5, right gave 1 → 3 is the LCA |

**Result:** node 3

## Cost

O(n) time; O(h) recursion depth.

## The code (C#, compiled and tested against every part of the question)

```csharp
// TreeNode is provided by the starter (Models.cs): int Value; TreeNode Left, Right.

// LeetCode 236 — lowest common ancestor of two nodes in an ordinary binary tree (no ordering).
public static class LcaTree {
    public static TreeNode Find(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
        // Returns p, q, their LCA, or null — whichever of them lives in this subtree.
        if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
        TreeNode left = Find(root.Left, p, q);
        TreeNode right = Find(root.Right, p, q);
        if (left != null && right != null) return root;  // one on each side: this node is the split
        return left ?? right;                            // both on one side (or neither)
    }
}
```

## Likely follow-up questions

**Q: What if q might not be in the tree?**

The simple version would wrongly return p. Count how many of the two were actually found.

**Q: Complexity?**

O(n) time, O(h) recursion depth.

**Q: With parent pointers?**

Walk up from p into a set, then walk up from q until you hit the set — or the two-pointer list-intersection trick (LeetCode 160).

**Q: Shared state?**

Read-only tree.

**Q: A very deep tree.**

Iterative post-order, or parent map + ancestor set.

**Q: Many queries on the same tree.**

Binary lifting or Euler tour + RMQ.
